23. Write the position of sodium in the modern periodic table. Why is it known as alkali metal?
Ans:- Sodium is located in Group 1 (IA) and Period 3 of the modern periodic table. It is called an alkali metal because it
reacts with water to form a basic (alkaline) solution of sodium hydroxide.

25. In which group does Fluorine, Chlorine, and Bromine lie in the modern periodic table.
Ans:- Fluorine (F), Chlorine (Cl), and Bromine (Br) all lie in Group 17 (VIIA) of the modern periodic table, which is also
known as the halogen group.
26. If you are given a chance to make improvements in the modern periodic table, what changes would you make in it?
Explain with reasons.
Ans:- If given a chance to improve the modern periodic table, I would place hydrogen in a separate position above both
Group 1 and Group 17 to show its dual properties, as it is not a true alkali metal. I would also display the f-block elements
(lanthanides and actinides) more clearly in line with their periods instead of placing them separately at the bottom. These
changes would make the periodic table more accurate and easier to understand.
27. Inert gases are kept in group 0 of the modern periodic table. Why?
Ans:- Inert gases are kept in Group 0 of the modern periodic table because they are chemically stable and unreactive. Their
outermost electron shells are completely filled, which makes them inert and unlikely to form compounds under normal
conditions.
28. Potassium is more reactive than sodium. Why?
Ans:- Potassium is more reactive than sodium because it is lower in Group 1 of the periodic table. Its outermost electron is
farther from the nucleus and is less tightly held due to weaker electrostatic attraction, so it is lost more easily during
reactions, making potassium more reactive.
29. The size of atoms decreases on going from left to right of a period in the periodic table. Why?
Ans:- The size of atoms decreases from left to right across a period because the number of protons in the nucleus increases,
which increases the nuclear charge. This stronger attraction pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus, reducing the atomic size.
